message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for rasterizing images, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) with powerful, complex control logic, large caches, and sophisticated branch prediction. | Hundreds to thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput rather than latency. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC) with many features (branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution). | Simpler instruction set, often SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) capable. |
| **Execution model** | Serial or lightly parallel; each core can execute a single thread at a time. | Highly parallel; each core can run many threads simultaneously. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high memory bandwidth per core. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on high‑bandwidth shared memory (VRAM). |
| **Typical workloads** | Single‑threaded or lightly threaded tasks, complex branching, I/O, OS services. | Tasks that can be split into many independent operations: image/video processing, scientific simulations, machine learning inference/training, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Latency vs throughput** | Optimized for low latency (fast response to a single request). | Optimized for high throughput (many operations per second). |
| **Programming model** | Traditional programming languages (C/C++, Java, etc.) with standard threading libraries. | Requires specialized APIs (CUDA, OpenCL, DirectX, Vulkan) or frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch) that expose parallelism. |
| **Energy efficiency** | More power‑hungry per core due to complex logic. | More efficient per FLOP because of simpler, highly parallel design. |

### Why the difference matters

- **Performance**: For tasks that can be parallelized (e.g., matrix multiplication), a GPU can outperform a CPU by orders of magnitude because it can launch thousands of threads at once.
- **Flexibility**: CPUs can handle almost any task, including those with irregular control flow, whereas GPUs excel when the same operation is applied to many data elements independently.
- **Cost & Power**: GPUs provide higher performance per watt for parallel workloads, but CPUs are cheaper and more versatile for general use.

In practice, modern systems combine both: the CPU handles the “control” side (running the OS, managing I/O, orchestrating tasks), while the GPU accelerates the “data” side (heavy numeric or graphical computations). This synergy is especially evident in fields like deep learning, scientific computing, and real‑time rendering.
